blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — contaminated-linen handling
stem: A nurse is handling contaminated linen in a patient-care area. Which action is appropriate?

options.A: Handle the linen with minimal agitation and contain it at the point of use, using leak-resistant containment when blood or body fluids could soak through.
options.B: Sort the linen in the patient-care area before bagging so visibly contaminated pieces can be separated from other textiles before transport.
options.C: Prerinse heavily contaminated linen in the patient-care area before placing it in a closed transport bag to reduce soil sent to the laundry.
options.D: Shake the linen gently before bagging so loose debris is removed, then place it in a standard cloth bag even when body fluids could soak through.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC environmental infection-control recommendations direct healthcare personnel to handle contaminated textiles with minimum agitation, contain them at the point of use, avoid sorting or prerinsing them in patient-care areas, and use leak-resistant containment when blood or body substances could leak or soak through. B is incorrect because contaminated linen should not be sorted in the patient-care area. C is incorrect because contaminated linen should not be prerinised there. D increases agitation and also uses inadequate containment when soak-through is possible.
educational_objective: Handle contaminated healthcare linen with minimum agitation, contain it at the point of use, avoid sorting or prerinsing it in patient-care areas, and use leak-resistant containment when indicated.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Part II. Recommendations for Environmental Infection Control in Health-Care Facilities; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: CDC recommendations page dated January 11, 2024 and live-currentness rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC Environmental Infection Control Recommendations, Laundry and Bedding, G.III Routine Handling of Contaminated Laundry, lines 558-563: minimum agitation; contain at point of use; do not sort or prerinse in patient-care areas; use leak-resistant containment for blood/body-substance contamination.
source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports minimum agitation, point-of-use containment, no sorting or prerinsing in patient-care areas, and leak-resistant containment when contaminated textiles can leak or soak through.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: apply infection-prevention principles and protect clients and health care personnel from environmental hazards.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — the official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; CDC evidence for the key is current HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; combines the required low-agitation, point-of-use containment, and leak-resistant containment principles.
option_audit.B: Plausible sorting workflow but incorrect because sorting contaminated textiles in patient-care areas is specifically prohibited.
option_audit.C: Plausible soil-reduction step but incorrect because prerinsing contaminated textiles in patient-care areas is specifically prohibited.
option_audit.D: Plausible debris-removal approach but incorrect because shaking increases agitation and standard cloth containment is inadequate when soak-through is possible.

cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified: B sorts in the care area, C prerinses in the care area, and D increases agitation while using inadequate containment for soak-through risk.
